objectives: Organize white-noise stimuli, spike trains, and the spike-triggered ensemble into a system-identification workflow, distinguishing a descriptive STA, a filter estimator, and a complete LNP component.
Move among continuous convolution, pixel-index summation, and matrix notation while tracking the shapes of S, K, L, and the count vector and the orientation of the time-lag axis.
Derive the normal equation and Hessian from mean-squared loss for a linear neuron, and explain circular versus elongated loss contours through stimulus covariance.
Starting from \(SS^\mathrm{T}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2I\), derive the proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and the STA while retaining the scaling by spike count, bin width, and stimulus variance.
Recover a static nonlinearity with the small-bin Poisson approximation and diagnose STA failure caused by multiple features, an even nonlinearity, colored stimuli, or insufficient data.
prerequisiteBridge: An LNP model first takes the inner product between stimulus-history vector \(s_{t}\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times 1}\) and filter \(K\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times 1}\), giving \(L_{t}=K^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\), and then maps \(L_{t}\) through nonlinearity F to a rate. P may flatten pixels together with x, y, and several past time lags into one index. Every experimental time bin supplies one column \(s_{t}\), so the design matrix is \(S\in \mathbb{R}^{P\times T}\).

Least squares chooses K so that \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) approximates measured response h. Its gradient is \(-S(h-S^\mathrm{T}K)/T\); setting it to zero gives \(SS^\mathrm{T}K=Sh\). The Hessian \(SS^\mathrm{T}/T\) describes loss curvature along filter directions. If one stimulus direction is scarcely sampled, its curvature is small and the filter estimate becomes highly noise-sensitive.

Here white noise means that distinct pixel/time dimensions are approximately zero-mean, uncorrelated, and equal-variance, so the large-sample covariance approaches \(\sigma _{s}^2I\). With sufficiently small bins, spike count \(k_{t}\) is usually 0 or 1 and \(P(k_{t}=1|L_{t})\approx \Delta tF(L_{t})\). The STA averages stimulus vectors preceding spike bins, all aligned to the same lags.

modules.title: White-Noise System Identification in Three Notations
paragraphs: System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. A standard protocol presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first.

The spike-triggered ensemble contains every stimulus vector that preceded a spike, and its mean is the STA. For an ON-center RGC, the most recent lag may show a bright center and dark surround, while an earlier lag may differ in sign or shape, producing a biphasic temporal kernel. Every history must be aligned to its spike; otherwise alignment error artificially smears the filter in addition to true latency variation.

Continuous notation writes \(L(t)=\int dx'\) dy' dt' \(K(x',y',t')s(x',y',t-t')\). After discretization, combine (x,y,t') into index p to obtain \(L_{t}=\sum _pK_{p}S_{pt}\). Matrix notation is \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\). All three forms express the same inner product. Matrix form is convenient for least squares, whereas continuous form shows spatial location and causal lag directly.

Each column of S is an entire stimulus history, not just the current frame; the p entries of K follow the same flattening order. Reversing the lag index flips the estimated kernel in time. A white-noise protocol matters not because the pattern merely looks random, but because different dimensions have nearly diagonal sample covariance on a common scale, reducing estimator bias and uneven uncertainty.
keyPoints: An STA requires identical stimulus-history alignment at every spike; averaging only the spike frame is insufficient.
Continuous convolution, a pixel sum, and \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) are alternative representations of the same calculation.
The defining benefit of white noise is covariance isotropy, not an arbitrarily generated noisy picture.

derivation.title: Discretizing Spatiotemporal Convolution as \(S^\mathrm{T}K\)
derivation.setup: Use \(N_{x}\times N_{y}\) pixels and \(N_\tau\) causal lags, for total dimension \(P=N_{x}N_{y}N_\tau\); the experiment contains T usable time bins.

steps.title: Define a Compound Index
steps.explanation: Assign a unique p to every \((x_{i},y_{j},\tau _{q})\), write \(K(x_{i},y_{j},\tau _{q})\) as \(K_{p}\), and write the past stimulus \(s(x_{i},y_{j},t-\tau _{q})\) corresponding to time t as \(S_{pt}\).

steps.title: Replace the Integral with a Grid-Volume-Weighted Sum
steps.explanation: Spatial and temporal discretization introduces the factor \(\Delta x\Delta y\Delta \tau\). Absorbing it into \(K_{p}\) leaves an ordinary dot product.

steps.title: Stack All Time Bins into a Vector
steps.explanation: \(S^\mathrm{T}\) is T×P; multiplying it by P×1 vector K produces T×1 vector L, with each row reproducing one time-bin inner product.

symbolNotes: In this lecture T denotes sample count but is also commonly used for physical time. Within matrix shapes it means the number of bins, and explanations should keep the meanings distinct.
The time coordinate of K is look-back lag: \(\tau =0\) is the current or most recent bin, and positive \(\tau\) refers to earlier stimuli.
derivation.unitsCheck: If continuous K has units drive/(contrast·area·time), multiplying by contrast and dx dy \(d\tau\) gives drive. If discrete K absorbs grid volume, its numerical units depend on binning.
derivation.limitCheck: A frame rate that is too low aliases fast temporal structure. A history window that is too short truncates the kernel; one that is too long increases P and reduces statistical power per dimension.

workedExample.title: Matrix Prediction with Two Pixels and Four Time Bins
workedExample.problem: Let \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\) and \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\). Compute \(L=S^\mathrm{T}K\) and interpret each entry.
steps: At t1 the stimulus is (1,1), so \(L_{1}=2\times 1+1\times 1=3\); at t2 it is (-1,1), so \(L_{2}=-2+1=-1\).
Therefore \(L=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). The first pixel has the larger weight, so changing its coordinate affects the drive more strongly.
workedExample.result: One matrix multiplication computes the filter projections for all four time bins while preserving the pairing with each stimulus column.
workedExample.sanityCheck: S is \(2\times 4\) and \(S^\mathrm{T}\) is \(4\times 2\); multiplication by \(2\times 1\) K must yield \(4\times 1\). A 2-dimensional result signals that the orientation has been reversed.

pitfalls: Flattening the stimulus without recording pixel and lag order, so the resulting vector cannot be reshaped correctly into a receptive field.
Calling a stimulus white merely because it looks random, without checking its mean, variance, cross-correlations, and finite-sample covariance.

modules.title: Least Squares, the Hessian, and White-Noise Isotropy
paragraphs: First consider a linear neuron \(h_{t}\approx K^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\), where h may be a measured firing-rate estimate. Mean-squared loss averages prediction error over T bins. Setting \(\mathrm{gradient}=0\) gives the normal equation \(SS^\mathrm{T}K=Sh\): stimulus covariance scale times the filter equals stimulus-response cross-correlation. Identifiability depends on whether S spans the relevant directions.

For a linear model with quadratic loss, the Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\) is independent of K. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of the loss ellipse and its eigenvalues are curvatures. Along a large-eigenvalue direction, a small change in K noticeably changes predictions and the data tightly constrain the minimum. Along a small-eigenvalue direction, the loss is flat and recording noise, finite samples, or regularization can move the estimate substantially.

In ideal Gaussian white stimulation, every \(S_{pt}\) has zero mean and variance \(\sigma _{s}^2\), and different p dimensions are uncorrelated. At large T, \((SS^\mathrm{T})_{pq}=\sum _tS_{pt}S_{qt}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2\delta _{pq}\). Consequently \(H\approx \sigma _{s}^2I\), the loss contours are nearly circular, and every filter dimension has equal curvature.

A finite dataset never has covariance exactly equal to the identity: off-diagonal sample covariances fluctuate around zero. Unequal pixel variances produce a diagonal but anisotropic H. With colored stimuli, correlations in H cause raw cross-correlation to mix the true filter with the stimulus spectrum. One must then apply the covariance inverse explicitly, whiten the stimulus, or fit a regularized likelihood model.
keyPoints: The normal equation expresses filter estimation as inverse covariance applied to stimulus-response correlation.
A Hessian eigenvalue measures both loss curvature and identifiability along its filter direction.
White-noise isotropy is a large-sample approximation; colored stimuli require covariance correction.

derivation.title: The Normal Equation and an Isotropic Hessian

steps.title: Compute the Gradient
steps.explanation: For residual \(r=h-S^\mathrm{T}K\), derivatives of prediction along the filter coordinates are supplied by S, so the gradient is -S times the residual.

steps.title: Compute the Estimate and Hessian
steps.explanation: Setting \(\mathrm{gradient}=0\) yields \(SS^\mathrm{T}K=Sh\). Differentiating the gradient once more gives \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\).

steps.title: Insert the White Covariance
steps.explanation: For independent, equal-variance dimensions, off-diagonal sample sums approach zero and diagonal sums approach \(T\sigma _{s}^2\), so the inverse is approximately \((T\sigma _{s}^2)^{-1}I\).

symbolNotes: H is a P×P curvature matrix; it is neither neural-response covariance nor spike-triggered covariance.
\(\delta _{pq}\) is the Kronecker delta: it equals 1 for \(p=q\) and 0 otherwise, encoding ideal white covariance.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) has units stimulus^2 and Sh has units stimulus×response. The resulting estimate therefore has units response/stimulus, as required for linear-filter gain.
derivation.limitCheck: If \(T\le P\) or stimulus dimensions are linearly dependent, \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) may be singular and the inverse expression cannot be used directly.

workedExample.title: Recovering a Known Filter from a White Design
workedExample.problem: Continue with \(S=[[1,-1,1,-1],[1,1,-1,-1]]\), true \(K=(2,1)^\mathrm{T}\), and \(h=S^\mathrm{T}K=(3,-1,1,-3)^\mathrm{T}\). Recover K by least squares.
steps: \(SS^\mathrm{T}=[[4,0],[0,4]]=4I\), showing that the two stimulus dimensions have isotropic sample covariance.
\(Sh=(8,4)^\mathrm{T}\); for example, its first entry is \(1\times 3+(-1)\times (-1)+1\times 1+(-1)\times (-3)=8\).
workedExample.result: For orthogonal equal-variance stimuli, the covariance inverse supplies only a common rescaling, so the direction of the cross-correlation is the filter direction.
workedExample.sanityCheck: If the second stimulus row is replaced by a copy of the first, \(SS^\mathrm{T}\) has \(\operatorname{rank} 1\). Only the sum of the two filter weights affects prediction, so the weights cannot be identified separately.

pitfalls: Interpreting a circular loss contour as a circular receptive field; the contour describes curvature in parameter space, not spatial shape.
Using the white-noise approximation without the large-T, equal-variance, and independence assumptions.

modules.title: From the Kernel Estimate to the STA, Nonlinearity, and Failure Diagnostics
paragraphs: The data contain spike counts \(k_{t}\) rather than a continuous rate \(h_{t}\). Choose bin width \(\Delta t\) small enough that \(k_{t}\in {0,1}\) usually holds and define rate estimate \(h_{t}=k_{t}/\Delta t\). Then Sh=(1/Δt)Σ_{t:k_t=1}\(s_{t}\), the sum of spike-triggered stimulus vectors scaled by bin width.

Because \(STA=(1/n_{sp})\sum _{spikes}s_{t}\), a white design gives \(\hat{K}\approx [n_{sp}/(T\sigma _{s}^2\Delta t)]STA\). STA and K point in the same direction, but absolute amplitude depends on spike count, recording duration, stimulus variance, and bin width. Comparing raw STA amplitudes across cells or conditions can therefore mistake a firing-rate change for a filter-gain change.

After estimating \(\hat{K}\), compute \(L_{t}=\hat{K}^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\) in every time bin, group values into bins of L, and estimate empirical \(P(\mathrm{spike}|L)\). The small-bin Poisson approximation gives \(P(k=1|L)\approx \Delta tF(L)\), hence \(\hat{F}(L)=P(\mathrm{spike}|L)/\Delta t\). Finally combine \(\hat{K}\), \(\hat{F}\), and the Poisson stage on held-out stimuli and compare predicted with observed spikes; a training STA alone is not a model test.

STA succeeds when one linear dimension dominates, the stimulus distribution is suitable, and spike count is adequate. Colored stimulation biases its direction; non-Gaussian input breaks the simple proportionality; multiple relevant dimensions collapse into one average; an even nonlinearity \(F(L)=F(-L)\) cancels +K and -K ensembles; and history dependence or adaptation contaminates the stimulus filter. Thus \(STA=0\) is not evidence for “no receptive field.”
keyPoints: The proportionality between \(\hat{K}\) and STA contains \(n_{sp}\), T, \(\sigma _{s}^2\), and \(\Delta t\); their directional relation is more robust than raw amplitude.
Estimate the nonlinearity by dividing projection-conditioned spike probability by bin width.
An even response, multiple relevant dimensions, and colored stimulation can bias an STA or make it zero.

derivation.title: STA Proportionality with All Scale Factors Retained
derivation.setup: Assume white stimulation \(SS^\mathrm{T}\approx T\sigma _{s}^2I\), bin counts \(k_{t}\in {0,1}\), rate estimate \(h_{t}=k_{t}/\Delta t\), and \(n_{sp}\) spike bins.

steps.title: Rewrite Response Cross-Correlation as a Spike Sum
steps.explanation: Bins with \(k_{t}=0\) contribute nothing; bins with \(k_{t}=1\) retain stimulus vector \(s_{t}\) and carry scale \(1/\Delta t\).

steps.title: Introduce the Definition of STA
steps.explanation: The spike sum equals spike count times the mean spike-triggered stimulus.

steps.title: Substitute the Least-Squares Estimate
steps.explanation: The covariance inverse contributes the common factor \(1/(T\sigma _{s}^2)\), yielding the proportionality between filter and STA.

symbolNotes: \(n_{sp}/T\Delta t\) is the mean firing rate, so the proportionality factor can also be written mean \(\mathrm{rate}/\sigma _{s}^2\).
STA entries have stimulus units. \(\hat{K}\) as a rate filter is additionally divided by stimulus variance, so their gain units differ.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(n_{sp}/(T\Delta t)\) has units 1/time; dividing by \(\sigma _{s}^2\) and multiplying by stimulus gives rate/stimulus, as required for a linear rate filter.
derivation.limitCheck: If bins are too wide, \(k_{t}\) can exceed 1 and the Bernoulli simplification fails. With too few spikes, STA variance is large even when the expectation relation holds.

workedExample.title: How an Even Nonlinearity Makes the STA Vanish
workedExample.problem: A one-dimensional stimulus s takes -1, 0, or +1 with equal prior probability. The neuron spikes with probability 0.4 at \(s=\pm 1\) and 0.1 at \(s=0\). Compute the spike-triggered mean and second moment and compare them with the original stimulus variance.
steps: The total spike probability is \((0.4+0.1+0.4)/3=0.3\). Bayes' rule gives \(P(s=-1|\mathrm{spike})=4/9\), \(P(s=0|\mathrm{spike})=1/9\), and \(P(s=+1|\mathrm{spike})=4/9\).
The positive and negative endpoints have equal conditional weight, so \(STA=E[s|\mathrm{spike}]=(-1)(4/9)+0+(+1)(4/9)=0\).
The spike-triggered second moment is \(E[s^2|\mathrm{spike}]=(4/9)+(4/9)=8/9\). Because the conditional mean is zero, this is also the spike-triggered variance.
The original stimulus has zero mean and variance \(E[s^2]=2/3\). Spike-triggered variance increases by \(8/9-2/3=2/9\), revealing a preference for large |s|.
workedExample.result: The STA is zero, yet spike-triggered variance rises from 2/3 to 8/9. STC or a quadratic model can detect the relevant direction hidden by symmetric averaging over signs.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The three conditional probabilities sum to 1. If the spike probabilities at ±1 are changed to equal that at \(s=0\), the spike-triggered distribution returns to the prior and the variance difference becomes zero.

pitfalls: Comparing raw STA amplitudes across conditions without correcting for spike rate, stimulus variance, duration, and bin width.
Reading \(STA=0\) as proof that a neuron is not stimulus-selective while ignoring even nonlinearities and multiple-feature coding.

figures.title: Forward LNP Prediction and Reverse STA Estimation Form One Validation Workflow
figures.alt: A flow diagram showing white-noise stimulus histories passing through a linear projection and nonlinearity to generate spikes, after which pre-spike stimuli are aligned and averaged to produce an STA parallel to the filter direction.
figures.caption: A forward LNP model projects stimulus history onto \(L=k^{\mathrm{T}}s\), transforms it through \(F(L)\) into a conditional firing rate, and generates spikes. Reverse analysis aligns and averages the stimulus history before each spike. For zero-mean white Gaussian input, one relevant dimension, and sufficient data, STA points along k. Colored input, an even nonlinearity, or multiple relevant dimensions breaks this simple relation.

synthesis: STA is both a descriptive average and, under a linear model, Gaussian white stimulation, and a suitable nonlinearity, a filter estimator. Matrix least squares reveals why: white stimulation makes the design covariance approximately a scalar identity, reducing the normal equation to a stimulus-response correlation. Recovering the nonlinearity yields an LNP model that can predict new stimuli, but multiple relevant dimensions, even-symmetric nonlinearities, or correlated stimulation can make the STA zero or biased.
workedExamples: 【例题】题目：两个实验 stimulus variance 不同，但 neuron filter 相同。

Worked solution. raw STA amplitude 会随 \(\sigma _{s}^{2}\)、rate/spike count 与 bin width 改变；比较 filter direction/normalized shape 前需按 derivation scale 或标准化。 Check. STA 是 filter 的 proportional estimator，不是无条件等幅度。
【拓展例题】题目：neuron 对 \(|K^\mathrm{T}s|\) 大时都放电。
Worked solution. spikes 前既有 +K-like 也有 −K-like stimuli，平均相消，\(STA\approx 0\)；STC 可找到 variance 增大的 K direction。 Check. \(STA=0\) 不等于没有 stimulus selectivity。

glossary.definition: Inferring a system model from input-output data.
An ideal random stimulus with uncorrelated dimensions or time bins and uniform power.
The collection of stimulus histories preceding all spikes.
The mean of the spike-triggered ensemble.
A matrix organizing stimulus vectors by examples or time bins.
The matrix of second derivatives of loss with respect to parameters.
Having equal curvature or variance in every direction.
Removing covariance correlations to obtain variables near unit covariance.
A stimulus whose dimensions have nonzero covariance.
A stimulus-projection direction on which the response depends.

commonTraps: Treating the STA only as an image average without specifying time-lag alignment.
Leaving matrix orientation unstated and confusing \(S^\mathrm{T}K\) with KS.
Omitting the large-sample and equal-variance assumptions behind white covariance.
Equating STA amplitude unconditionally with physical filter gain.
Concluding from \(STA=0\) that a neuron has no receptive field.
Forgetting to divide by bin width when recovering F.
Evaluating a model on its training fit instead of held-out prediction.
Distinguish the STA as a descriptive average, linear-filter estimator, and LNP-model component. They are related under particular assumptions, not unconditionally equivalent.

errata.lectureTitle: Spike-Triggered Averaging and White-Noise System Identification
errata.originalIssue: The isotropic Hessian is a large-sample approximation, not an exact finite-data equality.
errata.explanation: If pixel variances differ, H may be diagonal without being isotropic. With colored stimulation, correlations appear in H and raw cross-correlation mixes the true filter with the stimulus spectrum.

errata.originalIssue: The proportionality constant contains T, stimulus variance, \(\Delta t\), and spike count; it cannot be omitted when comparing absolute gain.

questions.stem: Why must each member of the spike-triggered ensemble contain a stimulus history rather than only the frame in which the spike occurs?

choices.text: Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly.
Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise.
Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time.
Flattening the stimulus without recording pixel and lag order, so the resulting vector cannot be reshaped correctly into a receptive field.

questions.explanation: Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time. A history vector permits simultaneous estimation of spatial and temporal receptive-field structure. System identification reverses forward prediction. A forward LNP model predicts spikes from known K and F; the experiment supplies stimulus s and spikes k and seeks K and F. A standard protocol presents random checkerboard white noise, records neural spikes, looks backward from every spike over the same time lags, and averages those stimulus histories. Stimulus coordinates, frame duration, and neural latency must be defined first.

questions.stem: Why does an elongated loss contour indicate that some filter combinations are estimated unreliably?

choices.text: Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time.
Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise.
Interpreting a circular loss contour as a circular receptive field; the contour describes curvature in parameter space, not spatial shape.
Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly.

questions.explanation: Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly. This is a small-eigenvalue direction of the Hessian, where many different K values make similar predictions on the sampled stimuli, allowing finite noise to shift the minimum substantially. For a linear model with quadratic loss, the Hessian \(H=SS^\mathrm{T}/T\) is independent of K. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of the loss ellipse and its eigenvalues are curvatures. Along a large-eigenvalue direction, a small change in K noticeably changes predictions and the data tightly constrain the minimum. Along a small-eigenvalue direction, the loss is flat and recording noise, finite samples, or regularization can move the estimate substantially.

questions.stem: Why is a smooth increasing \(\hat{F}(L)\) curve on the training data insufficient evidence that an LNP model predicts?

choices.text: Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise.
Neural responses have latency and may depend on multiple past lags. Using only the current frame discards temporal filtering and attaches the causal feature to the wrong spike time.
Moving along the ellipse's long axis raises loss only slightly.
Comparing raw STA amplitudes across conditions without correcting for spike rate, stimulus variance, duration, and bin width.

questions.explanation: Both K and F were estimated from the same data, and binning plus a flexible curve can absorb noise. Generalization must be tested by computing projections on held-out stimuli and predicting conditional rates or spikes there. After estimating \(\hat{K}\), compute \(L_{t}=\hat{K}^\mathrm{T}s_{t}\) in every time bin, group values into bins of L, and estimate empirical \(P(\mathrm{spike}|L)\). The small-bin Poisson approximation gives \(P(k=1|L)\approx \Delta tF(L)\), hence \(\hat{F}(L)=P(\mathrm{spike}|L)/\Delta t\). Finally combine \(\hat{K}\), \(\hat{F}\), and the Poisson stage on held-out stimuli and compare predicted with observed spikes; a training STA alone is not a model test.

questions.explanation: A forward LNP model projects stimulus history onto \(L=k^{\mathrm{T}}s\), transforms it through \(F(L)\) into a conditional firing rate, and generates spikes. Reverse analysis aligns and averages the stimulus history before each spike. For zero-mean white Gaussian input, one relevant dimension, and sufficient data, STA points along k. Colored input, an even nonlinearity, or multiple relevant dimensions breaks this simple relation.
